title: Implement Queue using Stacks / Stack using Queues.
shortTitle: Implement Queue using Stacks / Stack using Queues

s1_definition.profdef: Implementing a queue using two stacks means simulating first-in-first-out behavior with two last-in-first-out stacks, by pushing onto an input stack and transferring to an output stack only when needed, giving amortized O(1) per operation. Implementing a stack using queues means simulating last-in-first-out behavior with queues, typically by rotating a single queue on every push so the newest element sits at the front.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India token counter. A queue is first-come-first-served, but all the clerk has are two spring-loaded trays that only give back the top item (stacks). To serve the oldest customer first, when the serving tray is empty the clerk flips the whole intake tray into the serving tray, reversing the order so the oldest is now on top. The reverse problem uses waiting lines to fake a last-in-first-out pile.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two stacks make a queue by reversing order on transfer, and a queue makes a stack by rotating the newest element to the front on every push.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Implementing a queue using two stacks means simulating first-in-first-out behavior with two last-in-first-out stacks, by pushing onto an input stack and transferring to an output stack only when needed, giving amortized O(1) per operation. Implementing a stack using queues means simulating last-in-first-out behavior with queues, typically by rotating a single queue on every push so the newest element sits at the front.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India token counter. A queue is first-come-first-served, but all the clerk has are two spring-loaded trays that only give back the top item (stacks). To serve the oldest customer first, when the serving tray is empty the clerk flips the whole intake tray into the serving tray, reversing the order so the oldest is now on top. The reverse problem uses waiting lines to fake a last-in-first-out pile.

**One line to remember:** Two stacks make a queue by reversing order on transfer, and a queue makes a stack by rotating the newest element to the front on every push.

sections.s2_technical:
For a queue from two stacks, I keep an input stack and an output stack. On enqueue, I push onto the input stack, which is constant time. On dequeue or peek, if the output stack is empty I pour the entire input stack into the output stack one element at a time, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top of the output stack, then I pop or peek the output stack. I only transfer when the output stack is empty, so each element is moved at most once from input to output across its lifetime, giving amortized constant time even though a single dequeue that triggers a transfer is linear.

For a stack from a single queue, on push I add the new element to the queue and then rotate the queue by removing and re-adding every earlier element behind it, so the newest element ends up at the front. That makes push linear but pop and peek constant, because the front of the queue is always the most recently pushed element, which is exactly last-in-first-out order.

A senior nuance for the two-stack queue is that you must not transfer eagerly on every dequeue; transferring only when the output stack is empty is what preserves amortized constant time. A nuance for the stack-from-queue is choosing whether to make push costly or pop costly; the single-queue rotation makes push the expensive operation, which is a deliberate trade-off.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes customer service requests strictly in the order received, first come first served, but the only primitive available in a constrained embedded teller device is a stack. We must build fair first-in-first-out ordering out of stacks.

This is exactly how a queue from two stacks works. The transfer step reverses the stack order to recover arrival order.

Problem 2 — Each request must be served quickly on average even though occasionally a single serve triggers a bulk transfer.

This is exactly why we transfer only when the output stack is empty, so each request is moved at most once and the average cost stays constant.

The code will have a `StackQueue` class implementing a FIFO request queue from two `Deque` stacks, with `enqueue`, `dequeue`, and `peek`, and a runnable demo that enqueues request tickets and serves them in arrival order with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three enqueues, a peek, two dequeues, one more enqueue, then two dequeues.

Step 1: The three enqueues push REQ-SAV2001, REQ-CUR3001, REQ-SAV4002 onto the input stack. The input stack top is the newest, REQ-SAV4002, and the output stack is empty.

Step 2: `peek()` sees the output stack empty, so it transfers: it pops the input stack repeatedly and pushes onto the output stack, reversing the order. The output stack top becomes REQ-SAV2001, the oldest arrival, which peek returns.

Step 3: The first `dequeue()` pops REQ-SAV2001 from the output stack. The second `dequeue()` pops REQ-CUR3001. The output stack now holds only REQ-SAV4002, and the input stack is empty.

Step 4: `enqueue("REQ-CUR5003")` pushes onto the input stack, which is fine because it does not disturb the output stack ordering.

Step 5: The next `dequeue()` finds the output stack non-empty and returns REQ-SAV4002 without transferring. The final `dequeue()` finds the output stack empty, transfers REQ-CUR5003 over, and returns it, preserving overall arrival order.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 13:15:00 INFO    peek (oldest) -> REQ-SAV2001
2026-10-27 13:15:00 INFO    serve -> REQ-SAV2001
2026-10-27 13:15:00 INFO    serve -> REQ-CUR3001
2026-10-27 13:15:00 INFO    serve -> REQ-SAV4002
2026-10-27 13:15:00 INFO    serve -> REQ-CUR5003
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  enqueue SAV2001, CUR3001, SAV4002
    │ input (top→bottom): [SAV4002, CUR3001, SAV2001]   output: []
    ▼
  peek / dequeue → output empty → TRANSFER
    │ pour input into output, reversing
    │ output (top→bottom): [SAV2001, CUR3001, SAV4002]
    ▼
  dequeue SAV2001, dequeue CUR3001       output: [SAV4002]
    │
  enqueue CUR5003                        input: [CUR5003]
    ▼
  dequeue SAV4002 (no transfer)          output: []
  dequeue → transfer CUR5003 → serve     FIFO preserved
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — StackQueue ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns / Principles ───────────────────────────┐
  │  Two LIFO stacks simulate one FIFO queue                 │
  │  Lazy transfer (only when output empty) → amortized O(1) │
  │  S (SOLID): StackQueue only provides FIFO semantics      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            StackQueue                 │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - input: Deque<String>               │  enqueue side
  │  - output: Deque<String>              │  dequeue side
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + enqueue(ticket): void              │  O(1)
  │  + dequeue(): String                  │  amortized O(1)
  │  + peek(): String                     │  amortized O(1)
  │  - shiftIfNeeded(): void              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for dequeue():
    Pre:  at least one element across both stacks
    Post: oldest element removed; transfer only if output was empty
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Implementing a queue using two stacks is about recreating first-in-first-out behavior using only last-in-first-out primitives, and the elegant solution keeps an input stack and an output stack. Every enqueue just pushes onto the input stack, which is constant time. Every dequeue or peek first checks the output stack, and only if it is empty does it pour the entire input stack into the output stack one element at a time, which reverses the order so the oldest element rises to the top, and then it pops or peeks the output stack.

The reason this is efficient is the lazy transfer rule. Because I transfer only when the output stack is empty, each element moves from the input stack to the output stack at most once in its lifetime, so even though one particular dequeue that triggers a transfer is linear, the cost spread across all operations is amortized constant time. If I naively transferred back and forth on every operation, I would destroy that guarantee.

The mirror problem, implementing a stack using queues, flips the trade-off. With a single queue I make push the expensive operation by adding the new element and then rotating every earlier element behind it, so the newest element sits at the front and pop and peek become constant time. The deliberate choice there is which operation to make costly, and the single-queue rotation pushes that cost onto push.

In my project at National Bank of India, a constrained teller intake component exposed only stack primitives, yet customer service requests had to be served strictly in arrival order. Building a first-in-first-out queue from two stacks with the lazy transfer rule gave us fair ordering with amortized constant-time serving, so a single occasional bulk transfer never hurt the overall throughput of the request-handling path.
